title: The Hubble radius, the cosmic horizon, and the Schwarzschild radius are not the same concept
text: First distinguish the scales: the Hubble radius is R_H=c/H(t); in a spatially flat FLRW universe, substituting the critical density ρ_c=3H²/(8πG) into the mass-energy inside the Hubble sphere M=(4π/3)ρ_cR_H³ yields 2GM/c²=R_H. This equality comes from the Friedmann equations; it is not two numbers that happen to be equal today, and it does not prove that the universe is a Schwarzschild black hole. The Schwarzschild solution describes a static, spherically symmetric, externally vacuum, asymptotically flat spacetime; FLRW describes a dynamic, approximately homogeneous and isotropic universe. The Hubble radius, the cosmological apparent horizon, the particle horizon, and the event horizon must be stated separately and cannot be lumped together as the radius of the observable universe.

title: Black-hole universes and parent universes are a family of hypotheses, not an established conclusion
text: "Our universe was born inside a black hole in another universe" is not simply a synonym for the multiverse, but a family of concrete yet unconfirmed models. Different versions use patching of classical general relativity, black-hole interior cosmology, or, in Einstein-Cartan theory, torsion to replace the singularity with a bounce. The preceding-level universe that produced the black hole can be colloquially called the parent universe, but one must first ask the user which model they mean; existing research shows that it can be constructed mathematically, which does not mean observations have proven that our universe actually originated this way.

title: Mass and weight
text: m is the source of inertia and gravity; W=m g is the force in the gravitational field where the object is; the two are proportional only when g is fixed. The most easily confused step: using kg as a unit of force; still saying on the Moon that 'my weight hasn't changed.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Work and energy
text: W=∫F·dx is a transfer process; E is a state quantity; the work done by a conservative force equals the change in kinetic energy. The most easily confused step: treating 'did work' and 'has energy' as the same thing; saying 'this object has a lot of work.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Force and momentum
text: F=dp/dt is the rate of change of momentum; F=ma holds only when mass is constant (it does not hold for a rocket). The most easily confused step: continuing to use F=ma in a variable-mass system. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Torque and energy
text: τ=r×F is a vector and depends on the choice of pivot; energy is a scalar and is independent of the pivot. The most easily confused step: writing the unit of torque N·m as J. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Inertial mass and gravitational mass
text: The m in F=ma and the m in F=GMm/r² are two independently defined quantities; their equivalence is an experimental fact (the equivalence principle), not a definition. The most easily confused step: treating the two as equal by logical necessity. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Centrifugal force and centripetal force
text: In an inertial frame there is only the centripetal force m v²/r pointing toward the center of the circle; 'centrifugal force' appears only in a rotating reference frame. The most easily confused step: saying in an inertial frame that one is 'flung out by centrifugal force.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Temperature and heat
text: T is a state quantity (a measure of the average molecular kinetic energy), Q is a process quantity (heat transferred); in Q=C ΔT temperature is the cause, not the content. The most easily confused step: saying 'this object has a lot of heat'; treating temperature as a stock of energy. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Heat and internal energy
text: Internal energy U is a state function, Q and W are path functions; ΔU=Q+W states only the change. The most easily confused step: saying 'how much heat the object contains.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Entropy and 'disorder'
text: S=k lnΩ counts the number of accessible microstates; 'disorder' is a metaphor, and two different arrangements may have equally large Ω. The most easily confused step: equating entropy directly with visual messiness. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Temperature and average molecular kinetic energy
text: For a monatomic ideal gas, (3/2)kT is the average translational kinetic energy; for polyatomic gases the rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom must also be counted. The most easily confused step: using (3/2)kT for all gases. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Carnot efficiency and real efficiency
text: η=1−Tc/Th is the reversible upper bound; a real machine can only be lower; it contains no power, and no time. The most easily confused step: using the Carnot efficiency to compute the actual output power. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Charge and current
text: q is a state quantity (coulomb), I=dq/dt is a flow (ampere); 1 C=1 A·s. The most easily confused step: confusing the ampere and the coulomb as the same quantity. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Electric field and electric potential
text: E=−∇V is a vector field, V is a scalar potential; on an equipotential surface E is not zero, only its tangential component is zero. The most easily confused step: inferring 'the electric field is zero' from 'the potential is zero.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: B and H
text: B is the magnetic flux density (including the medium's response), H is the magnetic field strength (defined by free currents); in vacuum B=μ0H. The most easily confused step: treating B and H as the same quantity in a ferromagnet. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Resistance and resistivity
text: R is a property of the device (Ω), ρ is a property of the material (Ω·m); R=ρL/A shows that the same material cut into different shapes has different R. The most easily confused step: saying 'the resistance of copper is 5 ohms.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Phase velocity and group velocity
text: v_p=ω/k is the velocity of points of equal phase, v_g=dω/dk is the speed at which energy and information propagate; in a dispersive medium the two are not equal, and v_g cannot exceed c. The most easily confused step: using a superluminal phase velocity to argue that information travels faster than light. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Frequency and wavelength
text: When the medium changes, f stays the same (it is set by the source), while λ changes together with v; c=fλ holds only in vacuum. The most easily confused step: saying 'when light enters water its frequency decreases.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Amplitude and intensity
text: I∝A²; doubling the amplitude makes the intensity four times larger, and sound pressure level uses a logarithm because of this squared relationship. The most easily confused step: adding decibels as if they were a linear scale. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Interference and diffraction
text: Both come from phase superposition; 'interference' emphasizes the superposition of multiple beams, 'diffraction' emphasizes the phase redistribution caused by boundaries, and the physical mechanism is the same. The most easily confused step: treating them as two different mechanisms. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: The uncertainty principle and 'measurement disturbance'
text: ΔxΔp≥ℏ/2 is an intrinsic property of the state (Fourier duality), not 'bumping into it with a photon and knocking it off course.' The most easily confused step: explaining the uncertainty principle by measurement disturbance. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Superposition and mixture
text: Superposition is the addition of amplitudes within a single state (with interference terms); a mixture is a classical probability weighting (with no interference terms). To judge a mixed state, look at the rank or purity of the density matrix: a mixed state has rank greater than 1 (Tr(ρ²)<1), a pure state satisfies ρ²=ρ (rank 1); diagonalizability is not the criterion—both pure and mixed states are Hermitian operators and both can be diagonalized, and the off-diagonal terms depend on the choice of basis. The most easily confused step: treating 'I don't know which one it is' as superposition. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Entanglement and superluminal communication
text: Entanglement gives correlations, but the results of local measurements are each random; to see the correlations one must exchange classical information. The most easily confused step: claiming that entanglement allows messages to travel faster than light. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Spin and 'rotation'
text: Spin is intrinsic angular momentum and has no classical counterpart; an electron's 'surface speed' computed as rotation would far exceed the speed of light. The most easily confused step: imagining spin as a small ball rotating. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Virtual particles and real particles
text: A virtual particle is an internal line in the perturbation expansion and is off-shell; treating an internal line as a real particle and asking 'where did it come from' asks the wrong question. The most easily confused step: using virtual particles to explain 'things in the vacuum appear out of nothing.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Time dilation and 'clocks running slow'
text: Δt=γΔτ says that the proper time between two events is the shortest; 'seeing' additionally superposes aberration and the Doppler effect. The most easily confused step: mixing observational effects with time dilation. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Rest mass and relativistic mass
text: In E²=(pc)²+(mc²)², m is the invariant rest mass; calling γm 'relativistic mass' contaminates the form of F=ma. The most easily confused step: saying 'the faster it goes the more mass it has, so it cannot exceed the speed of light.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Gravity and spacetime curvature
text: Newtonian gravity is the weak-field, low-speed limit; in the language of curvature, free fall is a geodesic, and there is no 'gravity' force. The most easily confused step: using curvature to explain things other than tides without checking the approximation. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: The Hubble radius, the cosmic horizon, and the Schwarzschild radius
text: R_H=c/H is a scale, the horizon is a causal structure; in FLRW, 2GM/c²=R_H comes from the Friedmann equations and does not prove that the universe is a black hole. The most easily confused step: lumping the three radii together as 'the radius of the observable universe.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Redshift and distance
text: Cosmological redshift comes from the scale factor 1+z=a0/a, not from the Doppler effect; converting to distance via Hubble's law requires stating which distance is used. The most easily confused step: using the Doppler formula to compute the velocity of a high-redshift object. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Dark energy and dark matter
text: Dark matter clumps (it has gravity, no electromagnetism), dark energy is approximately uniform (negative pressure, drives acceleration); the two act in opposite ways. The most easily confused step: treating them as the same kind of 'invisible stuff.' When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Characteristic time and mean time
text: In order-of-magnitude estimates τ~L/v is a characteristic time; 'mean' requires specifying the distribution over which the average is taken. The most easily confused step: passing off an estimated characteristic time as a statistical mean. When judging, first ask which layer it is—definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Friction and Friction-Generated Heat
text: f=μN gives a force; the heat generated is f times the relative displacement, so a large force does not mean a lot of heat. The easiest step to conflate: inferring the amount of heat released directly from the magnitude of friction. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Elastic vs. Plastic Deformation
text: In the elastic region stress is proportional to strain (Hooke's law), while the plastic region is irreversible; after the yield point, unloading does not return to the original position. The easiest step to conflate: continuing to use F=kx in the plastic region. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Pressure vs. Force
text: p=F/A is an intensive quantity, F is an extensive quantity; the same body weight on high heels and on skis differs in pressure by more than a factor of ten. The easiest step to conflate: saying that the greater the pressure, the greater the force. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Kinetic vs. Potential Energy
text: Kinetic energy depends on the reference frame (v is relative), potential energy depends on the choice of zero point; only their sum and their difference have physical meaning. The easiest step to conflate: asking what the potential energy is on its own without specifying the zero point. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Escape Velocity vs. Orbital Velocity
text: For a circular orbit v=√(GM/r), for escape v=√(2GM/r); the latter is √2 times the former, not 2 times. The easiest step to conflate: taking escape velocity to be twice the orbital velocity. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Temperature vs. Pressure
text: The ideal gas law pV=nRT connects the two, but under isothermal compression the temperature stays constant while the pressure rises. The easiest step to conflate: inferring a rise in temperature from a rise in pressure. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Reversible vs. Real Processes
text: Reversible is a limit (infinitely slow, no dissipation); real processes generate entropy, and a calculation along a reversible path gives an upper bound. The easiest step to conflate: using the reversible formula to compute the output of an actual engine. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Specific Heat vs. Latent Heat
text: Q=mcΔT is what raising the temperature requires, Q=mL is what a phase change requires, and there the temperature does not change. The easiest step to conflate: using mcΔT to compute the heat during a phase-change stage. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Free Energy vs. Internal Energy
text: F=U−TS (isothermal, isochoric) and G=U−TS+pV (isothermal, isobaric) are the quantities that determine spontaneity; U itself cannot. The easiest step to conflate: using a decrease in internal energy to judge whether a reaction can be spontaneous. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Electric Field Strength vs. Electric Field Energy Density
text: E is the field strength (V/m), u=½ε0E² is the energy density (J/m³); the two differ by one square and by the permittivity. The easiest step to conflate: using field strength as energy. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Capacitor vs. Battery
text: A capacitor stores charge and electric field energy (Q=CV), a battery does chemical work to maintain a potential difference. The easiest step to conflate: saying that a discharging capacitor provides a constant voltage. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Motional EMF vs. Induced EMF
text: Motional EMF comes from a conductor moving in a magnetic field (Lorentz force), induced EMF comes from a magnetic field changing with time (Faraday); one formula, two mechanisms. The easiest step to conflate: taking both to be a changing magnetic field. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Dielectric vs. Conductor
text: Inside a conductor E=0 (free charges rearrange), a dielectric only polarizes and inside it E≠0; the latter uses ε=εrε0. The easiest step to conflate: also saying the internal field is zero inside a dielectric. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Resonance vs. Beats
text: Resonance is when the driving frequency approaches the natural frequency (the amplitude is amplified), beats are the superposition of two nearby frequencies (the amplitude varies slowly). The easiest step to conflate: taking beats for a resonance phenomenon. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Refraction vs. Dispersion
text: Refraction is the change of speed at an interface (Snell's law), dispersion is v varying with frequency in the same medium; a prism splitting light is the latter. The easiest step to conflate: using Snell's law to explain a prism splitting light. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Linear Superposition vs. Nonlinear Effects
text: In a linear system two waves do not disturb each other (superposition principle), in a nonlinear one they mix frequencies and generate new frequencies. The easiest step to conflate: applying the superposition principle to intense laser light or intense sound waves. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Polarization vs. Intensity
text: Polarization is the direction of oscillation, intensity is the energy flow; Malus's law I=I0cos²θ describes how the former affects the latter. The easiest step to conflate: treating a polarizer as a filter with adjustable intensity. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Measurement vs. Wavefunction Collapse
text: Collapse is an additional postulate in the Copenhagen interpretation, not content of the Schrödinger equation; decoherence explains why no interference is seen. The easiest step to conflate: describing collapse as a result computed from the equation. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Tunneling vs. Passing Through a Wall
text: The tunneling probability decays exponentially with barrier width (~e^(−2κL)); it is not that anything can get through as long as it has energy. The easiest step to conflate: describing tunneling as a violation of energy conservation. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Pauli Exclusion vs. Electron Shells
text: The Pauli principle explains why electrons do not collapse into the nucleus and why shells exist; the Coulomb force provides the binding. The easiest step to conflate: describing shell structure as a direct result of the Coulomb force. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Relativity of Simultaneity vs. Time Dilation
text: The relativity of simultaneity is a coordinate convention (different inertial frames have different slices), time dilation is a comparison with proper time; the former gives rise to the latter. The easiest step to conflate: treating the two as two independent effects. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Doppler Redshift vs. Cosmological Redshift
text: The former comes from relative velocity (including the transverse effect), the latter from the scale factor 1+z=a0/a; at high z the two differ numerically. The easiest step to conflate: using the Doppler formula to compute quasar distances. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Special and General Relativistic Effects in GPS
text: Special relativity makes the satellite-borne clock run slow (about −7 microseconds per day), general relativity makes it run fast (about +45 microseconds per day), for a net of about +38 microseconds per day. The easiest step to conflate: saying only that relativity makes GPS run slow. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Luminosity vs. Flux
text: L is the power emitted by the source (W), F is what is received per unit area (W/m²); only F=L/(4πd²) brings in distance. The easiest step to conflate: inferring greater intrinsic brightness from appearing brighter. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Black Hole Mass vs. Horizon Radius
text: The Schwarzschild radius r_s=2GM/c² is proportional to M; estimating the density from r_s gives a value that decreases as M grows. The easiest step to conflate: using r_s to compute the density and saying that a black hole has extremely high density. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Dark Matter vs. Modified Gravity
text: The former adds matter (invisible but still gravitating), the latter changes the equations; the criterion is which one can explain more observations at the same time. The easiest step to conflate: treating modified gravity as an answer that needs no dark matter. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Order-of-Magnitude Estimation vs. Precise Calculation
text: The goal of order-of-magnitude estimation is to avoid gross error (within a factor of ten), only precise calculation pursues 1%; the two have different purposes and cannot substitute for each other. The easiest step to conflate: using an estimate as a conclusion, or demanding an estimate to three decimal places. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Models vs. Real Systems
text: A model always has assumptions (no friction, point mass, ideal gas); stating the assumptions clearly is stating the range of validity. The easiest step to conflate: taking a model's conclusions directly as conclusions about the world. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Correlation vs. Causation
text: Correlation only says that things are not independent; to speak of causation you need an intervention or a clear mechanism, and you must be able to state the counterfactual. The easiest step to conflate: drawing a causal conclusion directly from two data sets changing together. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Signal vs. Noise
text: The criterion depends on the signal-to-noise ratio and the sample size, not on whether there is a deviation; two standard deviations and twenty standard deviations are not the same thing. The easiest step to conflate: announcing a discovery from the deviation in a single observation. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Simulation Results vs. Experimental Verification
text: A simulation can only show that this set of equations behaves this way, not that the world behaves this way; the former rests on code correctness, the latter on measurement. The easiest step to conflate: using simulation results as experimental evidence. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Unit Conversion vs. Dimensional Analysis
text: Conversion changes the number (1 eV=1.602e-19 J), dimensional analysis changes the form (both sides must have the same dimensions); the latter can catch errors. The easiest step to conflate: using unit conversion in place of a dimensional check. When judging, first ask which layer it is — definition, approximation, or observational effect.

title: Which-Path Information and Measurement in the Double Slit
text: In the double slit the key is not “whether someone is watching” but whether which-path information enters the environment and becomes distinguishable. An interaction that can distinguish which slit the electron went through destroys the interference pattern, even if no one reads the record; if the detector can only partially distinguish the paths, the interference visibility drops partially rather than vanishing at once. Single electrons, landing one by one, still build up an interference distribution; it is not a classical trajectory in which the electron “goes through both slits at the same time”. What measurement changes is the system's distinguishable information and the way the subsequent probability amplitudes superpose, not consciousness or a line of sight. Distinguish experimental facts, mathematical predictions, and interpretation.
